FIRST WARN FORECAST
Friday, September 4, 2026

First. Accurate. Trusted.

EXTREME HEAT WARNING CONTINUES THROUGH SATURDAY

The late-summer heat wave continues today and Saturday, with another two days of dangerous heat across Missouri and Illinois.

The Extreme Heat Warning remains in effect through Saturday evening as afternoon temperatures climb into the middle 90s to around 100 degrees. Heat index values will generally range from 100 to 110 degrees, with the highest values occurring during the afternoon and early evening hours.

This is a prolonged heat event, and the combination of extreme afternoon heat and unusually warm overnight temperatures continues to create an elevated risk for heat-related illness.

Some improvement arrives Sunday, followed by a more noticeable break from the heat on Labor Day.

Unfortunately, the break will be brief.

Another round of potentially near-record heat is expected Tuesday and Wednesday.

FRIDAY: ANOTHER DANGEROUSLY HOT DAY

Very little change is expected in the overall air mass today.

Temperatures several thousand feet above the surface remain near the 99th percentile for this time of year, with 850-millibar temperatures around 21 to 23 degrees Celsius.

That supports another afternoon of temperatures in the middle and upper 90s across much of the First Warn Weather coverage area, with some locations approaching 100 degrees.

The St. Louis metropolitan area will again be particularly warm, and overnight temperatures will remain in the 70s. Some locations within the immediate St. Louis urban area may remain near 80 degrees overnight.

That limited overnight cooling is an important part of this heat event. When temperatures remain elevated after sunset, the body has less opportunity to recover before the next hot afternoon.

Heat index values today are expected to reach approximately 100 to 110 degrees.

Humidity will decrease somewhat during the middle and late afternoon as the atmosphere mixes deeply, but that will occur after the heat has already become dangerous.

ISOLATED SHOWERS POSSIBLE, BUT LITTLE RELIEF

Most of the region will remain dry today.

There is a small chance for an isolated shower or thunderstorm during the afternoon or evening, particularly across southeast Missouri and southwest Illinois.

The atmosphere is somewhat less capped in that area, and weak surface convergence could provide enough lift for an isolated storm.

Any storms that develop should be localized and brief.

They will not provide widespread rainfall or meaningful relief from the heat, and temperatures should remain largely unaffected.

SATURDAY: FINAL DAY OF EXTREME HEAT

Saturday will bring another day of dangerous heat before the weather pattern finally begins to change.

Temperatures should once again reach the middle and upper 90s, with some locations potentially approaching 100 degrees.

Heat index values will remain in the 100 to 110 degree range during the afternoon and early evening.

A weak backdoor cold front will begin moving into the region Saturday afternoon and evening. This boundary will approach from the east rather than from the northwest, which is why it is often referred to as a backdoor front.

The front may produce a few showers or thunderstorms, particularly across south-central and southwestern Illinois.

Rainfall coverage should remain limited. Current guidance only gives a relatively small percentage chance for measurable precipitation across the region.

Any showers or storms that develop should be isolated and localized.

More importantly, the front will finally begin changing our air mass.

SUNDAY: COOLER, BUT STILL WARM

Sunday will bring the first noticeable reduction in temperatures.

Behind the front, winds will turn more northeasterly as high pressure builds across the Great Lakes. Cooler air will gradually filter into Missouri and Illinois.

However, "cooler" is a relative term.

High temperatures Sunday will still reach around 90 to the middle 90s across much of the region, which remains 10 to 15 degrees above average for early September.

Humidity will be more complicated.

Some areas could temporarily hold onto higher dewpoints Sunday before a much drier air mass filters southwestward across the region.

Because of that moisture, portions of central and southeast Missouri could still experience heat index values near or above 100 degrees Sunday afternoon.

At this time, another heat headline is not expected for Sunday, but the forecast will need to be monitored as the front moves through.

LABOR DAY BRINGS A MORE NOTICEABLE BREAK

Monday, Labor Day, should finally feel considerably better.

Dewpoints are expected to fall into the upper 50s to middle 60s as the drier air mass becomes established.

Temperatures should also moderate, although it will remain warm for September.

The important difference will be the humidity.

Current guidance strongly favors heat index values remaining below 100 degrees across essentially the entire region.

For anyone with outdoor plans for Labor Day, Monday currently looks like the most comfortable day of the holiday weekend.

It may not feel like fall, but compared with the 100-plus degree heat indices we've experienced this week, it should be a welcome change.

THE HEAT RETURNS TUESDAY

Unfortunately, the cooler weather will not last long.

The upper-level ridge is forecast to begin building eastward again Tuesday, with heights increasing dramatically across the Mid-Mississippi Valley.

That will set the stage for another round of significant heat.

Temperatures are expected to climb back into the middle and upper 90s Tuesday, with some locations potentially approaching 100 degrees.

Wednesday could bring another very hot day as well, although the forecast becomes more uncertain because a cold front may begin approaching from the north.

If the front remains north of the region, significant heat will continue.

If it moves farther south and arrives earlier, temperatures could be somewhat lower, particularly across northeast Missouri and west-central Illinois.

For now, another period of potentially near-record heat is expected Tuesday into Wednesday.

WHAT HAPPENS AFTER WEDNESDAY?

This is where the forecast becomes considerably more uncertain.

Global forecast models are beginning to agree that an upper-level trough will move from the Northern Plains toward the Great Lakes during the middle of next week.

That should push the approaching front farther into the Mid-Mississippi Valley and weaken the ridge.

The eventual position of that front will become extremely important.

Areas south and southwest of the boundary could remain hot, while locations north and northeast of it could experience clouds, showers, thunderstorms, and cooler temperatures.

There is currently a large amount of uncertainty regarding exactly where that boundary will stall or whether it will completely move through the region.

So while another hot Tuesday and Wednesday are becoming increasingly likely, the forecast for Thursday and beyond remains much less certain.

HEAT SAFETY

The Extreme Heat Warning remains in effect through Saturday evening, and conditions will remain dangerous.

Drink plenty of water throughout the day and take frequent breaks if you are working or exercising outdoors. Avoid prolonged exposure during the hottest part of the afternoon whenever possible.

Check on older family members, friends, and neighbors.

Make sure pets have plenty of fresh water and shade. Remember that pavement can become dangerously hot during afternoons with temperatures near 100 degrees.

Never leave a child or animal inside a parked vehicle.

With several days of extreme heat already behind us, take symptoms of heat exhaustion seriously. Dizziness, weakness, headache, nausea, heavy sweating, and fainting can all be warning signs that the body is struggling with the heat.

THE BOTTOM LINE

The Extreme Heat Warning remains in effect through Saturday evening.

Friday and Saturday will bring another round of dangerous heat, with highs in the middle and upper 90s to around 100 degrees and heat index values between 100 and 110 degrees.

The St. Louis metropolitan area will remain especially warm overnight, with temperatures potentially staying near 80 degrees in the urban core.

A weak backdoor cold front arrives Saturday night, bringing some relief Sunday.

Sunday will still be warm, with highs around 90 to the middle 90s and some areas potentially experiencing heat index values around or above 100 degrees.

Labor Day Monday should provide a much more noticeable break, with lower humidity and heat index values expected to remain below 100 degrees.

Then the heat returns.

Tuesday and Wednesday are expected to bring another period of middle and upper 90s, with some locations potentially approaching 100 degrees and challenging daily records.

What happens after Wednesday remains uncertain as a cold front approaches and the upper-level pattern begins to change.

For now, the message is simple: we have two more dangerous days of heat ahead.

Take the Extreme Heat Warning seriously, stay hydrated, limit prolonged outdoor exposure, and give your body an opportunity to recover whenever possible.

severeNarrative:
First Warn Forecast & Severe Weather Outlook Update
11:50 AM CDT | Wednesday, June 17, 2026
First Warn Weather Alert Day
Headlines
Severe thunderstorms remain likely this afternoon and evening across Missouri and Illinois.
Damaging winds up to 85 mph, large hail up to 2.5 inches, and several tornadoes remain possible.
The greatest threat locally remains across eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois, including the St. Louis metro area.
Strong southwest winds will gust between 40 and 50 mph outside of thunderstorms.
Peak severe weather threat for the St. Louis area remains between 6 PM and 9 PM.

A potentially dangerous severe weather outbreak remains on track across portions of Missouri and Illinois this afternoon and evening. There has been little change in the overall forecast since this morning. The Storm Prediction Center continues to highlight much of eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois in an Enhanced Risk (Level 3 of 5) for severe weather, while portions of central Illinois remain under a Moderate Risk (Level 4 of 5) where the highest threat for significant severe weather exists.

An intense cluster of thunderstorms that developed overnight across Iowa produced wind gusts exceeding 90 mph and continues to influence the forecast across Illinois late this morning. The primary outflow boundary currently extends from far northeast Missouri into portions of south-central Illinois. This boundary will likely serve as a focus for severe thunderstorm development later today.

Strong sunshine south of the boundary is allowing temperatures to rapidly climb through the 80s while dew points remain in the upper 60s and lower 70s. Combined with an exceptionally strong wind field aloft, conditions remain favorable for supercells capable of producing all severe weather hazards.

While morning storms may slightly alter where the greatest risk ultimately develops, confidence remains high that numerous severe thunderstorms will develop this afternoon and continue through the evening hours.

Primary Threats

🌪 Several Tornadoes Possible

A few strong tornadoes remain possible.
Greatest tornado threat remains across central Illinois.
Tornadoes remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois, especially near any lingering outflow boundaries.

💨 Destructive Winds Possible

Widespread damaging winds of 60 to 80 mph.
Isolated wind gusts exceeding 85 mph remain possible.
Significant tree damage and widespread power outages could occur.

🧊 Large to Very Large Hail

Large hail remains possible with discrete supercells.
Hailstones up to 2.5 inches in diameter may occur.
Timing Across Missouri and Illinois
1 PM - 3 PM

The first severe thunderstorms are expected to develop across northeast Missouri and portions of west-central Illinois. Areas near Quincy, Kirksville, Palmyra, Hannibal, and surrounding communities should closely monitor conditions.

3 PM - 6 PM

The severe weather threat expands southeast into central Missouri and western Illinois. Columbia, Jefferson City, Mexico, Bowling Green, Troy, and portions of the northern St. Louis metro could see supercells capable of producing tornadoes, very large hail, and destructive winds.

6 PM - 9 PM

This remains the peak severe weather window for the St. Louis metropolitan area and much of eastern Missouri and western Illinois. Storms may become more widespread during this period while maintaining the potential to produce damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes. Residents from St. Louis and St. Charles to Edwardsville, Belleville, Alton, Farmington, and surrounding communities should be prepared to act quickly if warnings are issued.

9 PM - Midnight

Storms are expected to organize into a line extending from central Missouri into southern Indiana. Damaging straight-line winds become the primary threat as storms shift into southeast Missouri and southern Illinois. Heavy rainfall and localized flooding may also develop overnight.

Local First Warn Outlook

The highest confidence for severe weather today exists across the Enhanced Risk area covering much of eastern and central Missouri, including Columbia, Jefferson City, the St. Louis metro, northeast Missouri, and west-central Illinois.

Farther south, a Slight Risk extends across southern Missouri and southern Illinois, including Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon. Severe thunderstorms remain possible in these areas, but storm coverage and intensity may be somewhat lower than locations farther north.

The lowest severe weather threat remains across the Missouri Bootheel and far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border where a Marginal Risk remains in place. However, isolated severe storms cannot be ruled out.

Threat Levels

Greatest potential for strong tornadoes and destructive winds

Southwest Illinois

South-central Missouri
Southeast Missouri
Southern Illinois
Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon

Missouri Bootheel
Far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border
Areas south of Poplar Bluff and near Paducah
Additional Concern: Strong Winds Outside of Storms

Even outside of thunderstorms, strong southwest winds will continue through the afternoon. Sustained winds of 20 to 30 mph with gusts of 40 to 50 mph are expected. Loose outdoor objects should be secured, and travel may become difficult for high-profile vehicles.

Thursday Outlook

The cold front responsible for today's severe weather will gradually move south of the region overnight. Showers and a few thunderstorms may linger into Thursday, especially across southeast Missouri and southwest Illinois. Cooler temperatures in the 70s and lower 80s will provide a welcome break from today's heat and humidity.

Bottom Line

There has been little change in the forecast thinking since this morning. The atmosphere remains primed for severe thunderstorm development this afternoon and evening. While the greatest threat for strong tornadoes remains across central Illinois, all severe weather hazards remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois.

The St. Louis metro remains in the corridor for severe weather between 6 PM and 9 PM, with damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes all possible. Everyone across the First Warn viewing area should remain weather aware and have multiple ways to receive warnings throughout the day and tonight.
